questions.stem: In „Der Lehrer gibt dem Schüler das Buch“, which case is „dem Schüler“?
questions.explanation: „Dem Schüler“ is the indirect object, the person receiving the book, so it is dative. „Das Buch“ is the direct object in the accusative; the neuter article looks the same in nominative and accusative, which is why students mix the two.

questions.stem: Which case does „trotz“ take in standard written German?
questions.explanation: „Trotz“, „wegen“, „während“ and „statt“ take the genitive in written German: „trotz des Wetters“. The dative is heard in casual speech, but it is not the written standard.

questions.stem: Which form completes „Wegen d___ Regens wurde das Spiel abgesagt.“?
questions.explanation: „Wegen“ takes the genitive, and the masculine genitive article is „des“, with -s on the noun: „des Regens“. „Dem Regen“ is the colloquial dative, and it could not go with the genitive noun „Regens“ anyway.

questions.stem: Which form completes „Wir sind mit ___ gefahren.“ ('We travelled with the children')?
questions.explanation: „Mit“ takes the dative, the dative plural article is „den“, and a dative plural noun adds -n if it does not already end in -n or -s. „Den Kinder“ forgets the noun ending, which is the most common slip.

questions.stem: Which form completes „___ Tasche ist das?“ ('Whose bag is that?')?
questions.explanation: „Wessen“ is the genitive of „wer“ and asks about ownership. „Wem“ is the dative, 'to whom', and would need a verb such as „gehören“: „Wem gehört die Tasche?“

questions.stem: Which form completes „Ich habe gestern mit dem jungen ___ gesprochen.“ ('the young gentleman')?
questions.explanation: „Herr“ is a weak masculine noun, so it adds -n in every case but the nominative singular: „dem Herrn“. „Herren“ is the plural, which the singular article „dem“ rules out.

questions.stem: Which pair completes „Er geht in ___ Klassenzimmer und sitzt jetzt in ___ Klassenzimmer.“?
questions.explanation: With a two-way preposition, movement towards a place takes the accusative and position takes the dative. „Gehen“ is movement into the room, so „das“; „sitzen“ is where he is, so „dem“.

questions.stem: Which form completes „Hängst du das Bild an ___ Wand?“?
questions.explanation: „Hängen“ with an object is putting something somewhere, so „an“ takes the accusative, and „Wand“ is feminine: „an die Wand“. „An der Wand“ answers where the picture already hangs.

questions.stem: Why is it „auf dem Tisch“ in „Das Handy liegt auf dem Tisch“?
options: „Tisch“ is the indirect object of the verb „liegen“
„Liegen“ is one of the verbs that take a dative object
„Liegen“ describes position, so „auf“ takes the dative
„Auf“ is a preposition that always takes the dative
questions.explanation: „Auf“ is a two-way preposition: „liegen“ says where the phone is, so dative. With the movement verb „legen“ it would switch: „Ich lege das Handy auf den Tisch“.

questions.stem: Which preposition and article does „beim“ stand for?
questions.explanation: „Beim“ contracts „bei dem“, as „am“, „im“, „vom“ and „zum“ contract a preposition with „dem“. Plural „den“ never contracts, and „bei“ cannot take „das“ because it is always dative.

questions.stem: Which form completes „Am Sonntag fahren wir ___ Großeltern.“ ('to our grandparents')?
questions.explanation: „Zu“ takes the dative and „Großeltern“ is plural, so „zu den“. „Zum“ is „zu dem“ and „zur“ is „zu der“, both singular, and the plural article never contracts.

questions.stem: Which word completes „___ denkst du?“ ('What are you thinking about?')?
questions.explanation: The verb is „denken an“, so the question word is wo- plus „an“, with -r- added before a vowel: „woran“. The compound must match the verb's own preposition, which is why the others are wrong here.

questions.stem: Which word completes „Interessierst du dich für Fußball? – Ja, ich interessiere mich sehr ___.“?
questions.explanation: To refer back to a thing after a preposition, German uses da(r)- plus that preposition, so „für Fußball“ becomes „dafür“. „Für es“ is how an English speaker builds it word for word, and German does not use it for things.

questions.stem: Which question has the answer „Auf meinen Bruder“?
questions.explanation: For a person, German keeps the preposition and uses „wen“ or „wem“; „worauf“ is only for things. „Warten auf“ takes the accusative, so „auf wen“, not the dative „auf wem“.

questions.stem: In „Ich habe mich sehr darauf gefreut“, what could „darauf“ refer to?
options: A person the speaker was glad to see
Something in the past that the speaker enjoyed
The place where the speaker was waiting
A coming event, such as the holidays
questions.explanation: „Sich freuen auf“ is looking forward to something, and a da-compound stands for a thing, not a person. Being pleased about something already past is „sich freuen über“, so „darauf“ points ahead.

questions.stem: Which form completes „Ich nehme ___ Jacke hier, nicht jene dort.“?
questions.explanation: „Dieser“ takes the same endings as „der“, and „Jacke“ is feminine accusative, so „diese“. „Diesen“ is the masculine accusative, which would suit „den Mantel“.

questions.stem: Which form completes „Wir wohnen seit Jahren in ___ Straße.“ ('in the same street')?
questions.explanation: „Derselbe“ declines both parts: the article as „der“ and the ending as a weak adjective. „In“ here is position, so dative feminine: „der“ + „selben“. „Demselben“ would be masculine or neuter.

questions.stem: Which form completes „___ Schüler muss einen Ausweis mitbringen.“ ('Every student')?
questions.explanation: „Jeder“ is singular and takes „der“ endings, so masculine nominative „jeder Schüler“ with the singular verb „muss“. „Alle Schüler“ means the same, but it is plural and would need „müssen“.

questions.stem: What does „Manche Leute arbeiten lieber allein“ mean?
options: No one prefers to work alone
Some people prefer to work alone
Many people prefer to work alone
Most people prefer to work alone
questions.explanation: „Manche“ means 'some' or 'quite a few', not 'many', which is „viele“. „Lieber“ with a verb means 'prefer to': „Ich lese lieber“ is 'I prefer reading'.

questions.stem: What does „Hast du irgendeine Idee, wo er ist?“ mean?
options: Do you have any idea where he is?
Do you have another idea where he is?
Do you have the same idea where he is?
Don't you have an idea where he is?
questions.explanation: „Irgendein“ means 'some … or other' or 'any at all', so the question asks for any idea. 'Another idea' would be „eine andere Idee“, and the negative would need „keine“.

questions.stem: Which form completes „Das ist ___ Handy.“ ('That is her phone')?
questions.explanation: 'Her' is „ihr“, and „Handy“ is neuter nominative, so no ending: „ihr Handy“. „Sein“ is 'his' or 'its', and „ihre“ would suit a feminine or plural noun.

questions.stem: Which form completes „Der Film ist ___.“ ('The film is exciting')?
questions.explanation: An adjective after „sein“, „werden“ or „bleiben“ is predicative and takes no ending. Endings appear only when the adjective stands before its noun: „ein spannender Film“.

questions.stem: Which form completes „Es war ein ___ Spiel.“ ('It was a great game')?
questions.explanation: „Ein“ has no ending of its own in the neuter nominative, so the adjective shows the gender: „ein tolles Spiel“. „Das tolle Spiel“ takes -e because the article has already shown it.

questions.stem: Which form completes „Wir haben mit unserem ___ Nachbarn gesprochen.“ ('new')?
questions.explanation: After an article or possessive that already shows the dative („unserem“), the adjective takes -en. „Neuem“ repeats the -em, which only happens when there is no article at all.

questions.stem: Which form completes „Zum Frühstück trinke ich ___ Milch.“ ('cold')?
questions.explanation: With no article, the adjective takes the ending the article would have had: feminine accusative „die“, so „kalte Milch“. „Kalter“ would be masculine nominative, or the feminine dative and genitive.

questions.stem: Which form completes „Bei ___ Wetter bleiben wir lieber zu Hause.“ ('bad')?
questions.explanation: „Bei“ takes the dative, and with no article the adjective carries the article's ending: „dem“ gives „schlechtem Wetter“. -en appears only after an article that has already shown the case.

questions.stem: Which words complete „Das ist das Auto ___ ___ Bruders.“ ('of my older brother')?
questions.explanation: Possession here is genitive, and the masculine genitive of „mein“ is „meines“, with -s on „Bruders“. After an article that shows the case, the adjective takes -en: „älteren“.

questions.stem: Which phrase is correct in „Ich habe ___ gekauft.“ ('a new red bike')?
questions.explanation: Two adjectives in a row take the same ending. „Fahrrad“ is neuter accusative after „ein“, so both adjectives take -es; stopping the -es after the first adjective is the usual slip.

questions.stem: Which form completes „Nimm das ___ Stück!“ ('Take the bigger piece!')?
questions.explanation: The comparative of „groß“ is „größer“, with an umlaut, and before a noun it takes an adjective ending as well: „das größere Stück“. „Größte“ is the superlative, 'biggest'.

questions.stem: Which form completes „Das ist eines der ___ Restaurants hier.“ ('best')?
questions.explanation: „Gut“ is irregular: „besser“, „best-“. After „der“ in the genitive plural the adjective takes -en: „eines der besten Restaurants“, 'one of the best restaurants'.

questions.stem: How do you say 'she runs fastest' in German?
questions.explanation: Adverbs form the superlative with „am“ + -sten: schnell, schneller, am schnellsten. „Am schneller“ mixes the comparative into the superlative pattern.

questions.stem: Which sentence is correct in standard German?
options: Mein Bruder ist älter als ich.
Mein Bruder ist älter wie ich.
Mein Bruder ist mehr alt als ich.
Mein Bruder ist älter als mich.
questions.explanation: A comparison of difference uses „als“, and German forms the comparative with -er, not „mehr“. After „als“ the pronoun stays in the same case as what it is compared with, here the nominative „ich“.

questions.stem: Which form completes „Unsere ___ wohnen in der Schweiz.“ ('acquaintances')?
questions.explanation: „Bekannt“ used as a noun keeps its adjective endings. After „unsere“ in the plural the ending is -en; „Bekannte“ is correct only with no article, as in „Bekannte von mir“.

questions.stem: Which form completes „Er hat in seinem Leben viel ___ getan.“ ('a lot of good')?
questions.explanation: After „viel“, „etwas“ and „nichts“, an adjective becomes a neuter noun with the strong ending -es: „viel Gutes“, „etwas Neues“. It also takes a capital, because it is now a noun.

questions.stem: Which form completes „Ein ___ hat mir den Weg gezeigt.“ ('A German man')?
questions.explanation: „Deutsch“ as a person is an adjectival noun, so it declines like an adjective after „ein“: „ein Deutscher“, but „der Deutsche“. „Deutsche“ after „ein“ fits neither form; a woman would be „eine Deutsche“.

questions.stem: What gender is an infinitive used as a noun, such as „Lesen“?
options: The gender of the verb's object
questions.explanation: Every infinitive used as a noun is neuter and capitalised: „das Lesen“, „das Schwimmen“. That is how „Lachen tut gut“ works as a sentence: 'laughing does you good'.

questions.stem: What does „Sie muss das Lesen üben“ mean?
options: She has to read in order to practise
She has to practise the reading text
She has to read the exercise
questions.explanation: „Das Lesen“ is the activity of reading, an infinitive used as a noun, and it is the object of „üben“. A particular text would be „der Text“ or „das Lesestück“.

questions.stem: Which form completes „Wir freuen ___ schon auf die Ferien.“?
questions.explanation: „Sich freuen“ is reflexive, and the reflexive pronoun matches the subject: „wir … uns“. „Sich“ is used only for er, sie, es, Sie and the plural sie.

questions.stem: Which form completes „Ich wasche ___ jeden Morgen die Haare.“?
questions.explanation: When a reflexive verb already has a direct object, here „die Haare“, the reflexive pronoun moves to the dative: „ich wasche mir die Haare“. With no other object it is accusative: „ich wasche mich“.

questions.stem: Which word completes „Wie heißen die Leute, ___ uns begrüßt haben?“?
questions.explanation: The relative pronoun takes its gender and number from „die Leute“ and its case from its job in the clause. They did the greeting, so it is the subject: nominative plural „die“.

questions.stem: Which word completes „Der Film, ___ wir gestern gesehen haben, war spannend.“?
questions.explanation: „Film“ is masculine, and inside the relative clause it is the object of „gesehen“, so accusative „den“. „Der“ matches the gender but not the case, which is the usual mistake.

questions.stem: Which word completes „Das sind die Freunde, mit ___ ich nach Wien gefahren bin.“?
questions.explanation: „Mit“ takes the dative, and the dative plural relative pronoun is „denen“, not the article „den“. Relative pronouns differ from the articles in the dative plural and the genitive.

questions.stem: Which word completes „Der Mann, ___ Auto gestohlen wurde, rief die Polizei.“?
questions.explanation: The car belongs to the man, so the relative pronoun is genitive, and for a masculine noun that is „dessen“. „Deren“ is the genitive for a feminine or plural noun: „die Frau, deren Auto …“.

questions.stem: Which word completes „Er hat alles vergessen, ___ ich ihm gesagt habe.“?
questions.explanation: After „alles“, „etwas“ and „nichts“ the relative pronoun is „was“, and usually after a neuter superlative such as „das Schönste“ too. „Dass“ is a conjunction, not a pronoun, and cannot be the object of „gesagt“.
